source.title: AlignGuard-LoRA: Alignment-Preserving Fine-Tuning via Fisher-Guided Decomposition and Riemannian-Geodesic Collision Regularization
source.authors: Amitava Das; Abhilekh Borah; Vinija Jain; Aman Chadha

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some passages have extraction or formatting omissions, but the forgetting-scaling results in Table 6 are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits power laws for post-fine-tuning pretraining-loss increases in a fine-tuning/forgetting setting, rather than testing the original pretraining loss laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study varies fine-tuning token budgets and reports fitted loss curves and coefficients for standard LoRA and AlignGuard-LoRA. Its central scaling experiment keeps model size fixed, so it does not test loss scaling across parameter counts or compute. Results cited from other studies and unrelated alignment-retention results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The scaling section fits an adapted forgetting law: the rise in held-out pretraining loss against fine-tuning tokens, at one fixed model size. It uses the fit as a yardstick to compare the authors' own method (AlignGuard-LoRA) with standard LoRA. This is a different construct from any version. V1, V2, V3 and V6 concern pretraining loss falling with parameters, data or compute, or downstream predictability. V5 concerns the loss power law carrying into other regimes. Here loss rises with fine-tuning data, and the study does not check whether a power law fits better than other forms. Model size N is held fixed, yet an exponent α on N is reported for every domain. With fixed N that exponent cannot be identified from the data, so the fitted coefficients are not an empirical test of a power-law form. Mean relative fit errors of 0.25–0.85 also mean the reported fits do not show the loss following the law closely. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim AlignGuard-LoRA keeps the forgetting exponents α and β roughly unchanged while lowering amplitude A, residual E and fit error (MRE), for example on Arxiv MRE falls from 0.48 to 0.31. They describe this as flattening forgetting curves 'without compromising... scaling behavior'. They also claim the fitted coefficients can predict alignment robustness, but no result is shown for that. None of this tests the original pretraining scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: This study fits post-fine-tuning pretraining-loss increases against fine-tuning token volume at a fixed model size; it does not reproduce the original pretraining scaling experiments or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted coefficients vary by fine-tuning domain and method (Standard LoRA versus AlignGuard-LoRA). The paper also describes a fitting procedure using nonlinear least squares, Huber regression, and bootstrap resampling, but does not report alternative fitting-method results.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-fine-tuning pretraining loss rises with fine-tuning token volume (up to 2M–100M tokens) at a fixed model size (stated as 7B or 13B). Each of 12 domains is fitted with Lpt = L0 + A·D^β/N^α + E, separately for LoRA and AlignGuard. AlignGuard gives slightly smaller A, E and MRE. Fit errors are 0.25–0.85 MRE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning (pretraining-loss increase) scales as a power law in fine-tuning tokens, and is reduced by alignment-aware regularization.

record.problems: The scaling experiment holds model size fixed and therefore cannot establish parameter-count scaling or compute scaling. The text gives conflicting model sizes: 13B in Section 5.3 and Figure 10, versus LLaMA 3 (7B) in Appendix F.3 and elsewhere. It describes bootstrap uncertainty estimation but does not provide coefficient intervals in Table 6. Several reported MRE values exceed the paper's own 0.5 instability threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible Table 6 domain/method scaling results were omitted. The text's claimed forgetting-law relations involving model size are not rows because model size was fixed in the reported fitting setup; cited findings from earlier work and unrelated benchmark results were excluded.

untested.parts: Not tested: no pretraining runs varying parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs (the paper says none is performed beyond available data).
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

Not tested: no other modalities, no repeated-data runs, and no fine-tuning or transfer loss scaling with model or data scale. Only a forgetting curve at fixed N is fitted, and its exponent on N is unidentifiable.
Not tested: no downstream metrics against scale or loss.
Not tested: fitting choices are not varied. Coefficient differences between LoRA and AlignGuard come from fits of a different construct, with an unidentifiable α.

record.verdict_notes: Serious validity concerns. (1) N is fixed, yet α is reported per domain and the text claims α shows AlignGuard 'scales predictably with larger capacity'; this cannot be supported. (2) Model size is inconsistent: 7B in the appendix, 13B in the main text and Figure 10. (3) Only about 4 token budgets per domain are used to fit 4 parameters. No observed loss values are tabulated, and the Figure 10 curves are fitted projections. (4) The claimed amplitude reductions (20–50%) do not match Table 6, where most drops are about 5–16%, except Wikipedia at about 16%. (5) The forgetting-law source cited as Bethune et al. 2022 is not verifiable. Among the Kaplan/Hoffmann originals, only Hoffmann is cited, and only as inspiration.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures post-fine-tuning loss increase against fine-tuning token volume, not held-out pretraining loss scaling with pretraining parameters, tokens, or compute when the other axes are not bottlenecks.
It does not test whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs; it says no extrapolation beyond available domain data is performed.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is tested.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.

The study tests a fine-tuning/forgetting loss curve over fine-tuning token volume, but not image or video, repeated-data pretraining, or transfer scaling in the sense of the claim. It does not vary model size or compute.
The study does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.

The study reports domain- and method-specific fitted coefficients for forgetting curves, but does not manipulate fit procedure or parameter-counting choices, test compute-optimal allocation, or compare the original scaling-law studies.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The reported domain-specific fine-tuning/forgetting curves at the fixed model size
reader_labels.reason: The paper fits a power-law forgetting form against fine-tuning token volume across the listed domains; rows D1-L through D12-A report the fitted results. This supports only the tested fine-tuning-forgetting setting, not the original pretraining scaling claim.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dm mathematics, Enron emails, Github, Euro parl
reader_labels.reason: The reported LoRA MRE exceeds 0.5 for Dm mathematics, Enron emails, Github, and Euro parl, and the AlignGuard-LoRA MRE exceeds 0.5 for Euro parl; the paper itself treats MRE above 0.5 as a regression-instability flag (rows D2-L, D2-A, D3-L, D4-L, D7-L, D7-A).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Domain- and method-specific forgetting fits in the reported fixed-size fine-tuning setup
reader_labels.reason: The fitted coefficients vary across domains and shift between Standard LoRA and AlignGuard-LoRA, consistent with setup-dependent coefficients in this forgetting-law setting (rows D1-L through D12-A).
